name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Ashbridge, Duskreach`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`

`Rogue   — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

Along the far wall stretched the contract board, its notices pinned in uneven rows, a few of them curling at the edges. actions: 1. REGISTERS — pending: the Guild's registration fee is 2 silver (20 cp), one-time; a new member starts at Guild Rank Novice (the Guild's ranks run Novice to Legend); Power Rank (F to S) is a person's measured strength, a separate scale the Guild reads but never grants. Let the clerk name the fee and explain; stop there: he has not agreed to pay.

extra.display_text:
"Alaric Red." The clerk said it back as though testing the weight of it, then reached under the counter and set a ledger of his own on top, its spine cracked and its corners darkened by years of thumbs. "Guild registration. Fine. It's two silver, once, and it buys you this: a rank plate when you're measured, access to the contract board, the payout window, and the Guild's mediation if a client tries to cheat you. It does not buy you rescue. If something eats you in the field, we record it and move on." He opened the ledger to a fresh page and dipped his pen. "What we'll need is your name as you want it written, your age, and your Class, if you've been Assessed. If you haven't, the measuring stone in the back room will tell us what you are, and there's no charge for that — it's part of the fee." The pen hovered. "Power Rank comes off the same reading. The Guild reads it and writes it down; it grants you nothing. Two silver, and you walk out a Novice with a plate and a slip of paper." Behind Alaric, the man on the bench drew the knife along the whetstone once more and did not look up. Somewhere deeper in the hall a door opened and shut, and the smell of cold morning air came in with it and faded. The clerk waited, pen still poised over the empty line.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
"Alaric Red." The clerk said it back as though testing the weight of it, then reached under the counter and set a ledger of his own on top, its spine cracked and its corners darkened by years of thumbs. "Guild registration. Fine. It's two silver, once, and it buys you this: a rank plate when you're measured, access to the contract board, the payout window, and the Guild's mediation if a client tries to cheat you. It does not buy you rescue. If something eats you in the field, we record it and move on."

He opened the ledger to a fresh page and dipped his pen.

"What we'll need is your name as you want it written, your age, and your Class, if you've been Assessed. If you haven't, the measuring stone in the back room will tell us what you are, and there's no charge for that — it's part of the fee." The pen hovered. "Power Rank comes off the same reading. The Guild reads it and writes it down; it grants you nothing. Two silver, and you walk out a Novice with a plate and a slip of paper."

Behind Alaric, the man on the bench drew the knife along the whetstone once more and did not look up. Somewhere deeper in the hall a door opened and shut, and the smell of cold morning air came in with it and faded.

The clerk waited, pen still poised over the empty line.

extra.display_text:
He pulled the notice from the board and carried it to the counter. The clerk set down his pen, read it over, and pulled the ledger back toward himself. "Mossback Warrens, first level." He wrote the entry in a careful hand, then took a slip of stiff paper from a drawer, pressed it against the page, and the Guild seal rose on its face in faint brown ink. "Goblins hold it. Scouts mostly, on the first level, but scouts run and warn warriors, and warriors come in numbers. Half a day east, off the old quarry track — the hill with the moss over its mouth, you can't miss it if you keep to the track." He held out the slip. "The seal shows READY when the level's cleared. Bring the slip back to this counter and the payout window pays seventy copper against it. No trophies wanted, no counting done at the door — the seal knows." He glanced once at the staff leaning against the counter's edge, then back to the ledger. "The Warrens don't get lighter because you're a Novice. Folk go in pairs for a reason." The slip was in Alaric's hand now, the ink still smelling faintly of the press. Along the bottom, in small print: *Clear Mossback Warrens, Level 1 — Adventurers' Guild, Ashbridge.*

He pulled the notice from the board and carried it to the counter. The clerk set down his pen, read it over, and pulled the ledger back toward himself.

"Mossback Warrens, first level." He wrote the entry in a careful hand, then took a slip of stiff paper from a drawer, pressed it against the page, and the Guild seal rose on its face in faint brown ink. "Goblins hold it. Scouts mostly, on the first level, but scouts run and warn warriors, and warriors come in numbers. Half a day east, off the old quarry track — the hill with the moss over its mouth, you can't miss it if you keep to the track."

He held out the slip.

"The seal shows READY when the level's cleared. Bring the slip back to this counter and the payout window pays seventy copper against it. No trophies wanted, no counting done at the door — the seal knows." He glanced once at the staff leaning against the counter's edge, then back to the ledger. "The Warrens don't get lighter because you're a Novice. Folk go in pairs for a reason."

The slip was in Alaric's hand now, the ink still smelling faintly of the press. Along the bottom, in small print: *Clear Mossback Warrens, Level 1 — Adventurers' Guild, Ashbridge.*

extra.display_text:
The old quarry track left Ashbridge through the eastern gate, past the last vegetable plots and a boy driving geese, and then it was just ruts and gravel under a climbing sun. Cart traffic thinned as the road rose; twice wagons rolled past toward town, drivers giving the staff-carrying stranger a nod, nothing more. Gorse and low pines took the fields' place. By midday the town behind had shrunk to a grey smudge of rooftops and smoke. It was on a straight stretch, where the track ran between a bramble bank and a shallow ditch, that the ground told its story. A churned patch of mud at the track's edge — hoofprints, deep and splayed, more than one animal, pressed hard enough to have been made at a run. Around them, torn-up turf, and in the ditch a wheel rut half-caved in, its edge broken outward as if something heavy had gone down the slope in a hurry. A few paces farther on, a splintered piece of cart shaft lay in the grass, the wood pale and fresh where it had snapped. No cart, no animal, no people. The tracks ran off the track to the north, into the pines, and the ground there was too rootbound to hold a clear line. The Warrens' mossy hill sat farther east, an hour or more off still, a green hump just visible against the treeline on the horizon. The prints were recent — the mud at their bottoms still dark and wet.

ACTIVE SCENE — Carter · SHORT
The tracks held a line through the pines for a few hundred paces, hooves punching through needle litter, and then the trees opened on a hollow where the ground fell away to a streambed. The cart lay at the bottom of it. It had come down the slope sideways, slewed, and rolled. One wheel still turned slowly in the wind of the branches above, creaking. The other had come off and rolled farther, into the water. Crates had spilled across the stones — some split open on empty grain, a few intact, their lids staved in. The shafts pointed uphill at the sky. Of the animals there was no sign: the hoofprints left the wreck on the far side and ran north, unburdened, until the needle litter swallowed them. Harness lay cut, not torn — a knife had done that, quick and close to the leather. A man's boot showed under the tilted cart bed. The rest of him was pinned at the thigh, a heavy crate-iron bar across his leg where the load had settled. He was awake. At the creak of Alaric's step on the slope above, his head turned, and he went very still, eyes going first to the staff, then to the face above it. "Don't — " His voice cracked; he wet his mouth and tried again. "Don't come down fast. The oxen spooked at something back on the track. Something in the trees." He shifted, and the pain of it pulled a grunt through his teeth. "If it's still about, I'd as soon it didn't hear us talking." His leg was pinned well and truly; the bar would take two hands and a lever to lift, and he had clearly been trying it alone for a while — the mud around him was scuffed and stamped. A hand-axe lay just out of his reach, halfway down the slope where it had fallen. "I can pay," he said. "There's coin in my coat. Only get this off me."

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The tracks held a line through the pines for a few hundred paces, hooves punching through needle litter, and then the trees opened on a hollow where the ground fell away to a streambed. The cart lay at the bottom of it.

It had come down the slope sideways, slewed, and rolled. One wheel still turned slowly in the wind of the branches above, creaking. The other had come off and rolled farther, into the water. Crates had spilled across the stones — some split open on empty grain, a few intact, their lids staved in. The shafts pointed uphill at the sky.

Of the animals there was no sign: the hoofprints left the wreck on the far side and ran north, unburdened, until the needle litter swallowed them. Harness lay cut, not torn — a knife had done that, quick and close to the leather.

A man's boot showed under the tilted cart bed. The rest of him was pinned at the thigh, a heavy crate-iron bar across his leg where the load had settled. He was awake. At the creak of Alaric's step on the slope above, his head turned, and he went very still, eyes going first to the staff, then to the face above it.

"Don't — " His voice cracked; he wet his mouth and tried again. "Don't come down fast. The oxen spooked at something back on the track. Something in the trees." He shifted, and the pain of it pulled a grunt through his teeth. "If it's still about, I'd as soon it didn't hear us talking."

His leg was pinned well and truly; the bar would take two hands and a lever to lift, and he had clearly been trying it alone for a while — the mud around him was scuffed and stamped. A hand-axe lay just out of his reach, halfway down the slope where it had fallen.

"I can pay," he said. "There's coin in my coat. Only get this off me."

He stepped off the tracks and folded himself down behind a fallen pine, needles deep and silent, staff flat along the log. The greenish glow came on at its unhurried walking pace, swaying low to the ground, and the forest around it stayed exactly as quiet as before.

It resolved between the trunks at thirty paces: a goblin, small and stooped, carrying a lantern that burned a sickly green without smoke. It was naked but for a rag at its loins and a belt of strung teeth, and it did not search the ground or the trees — it walked the footprints' line straight as a plumb line, straight toward where the tracks began at the wreck. Its head turned once, a slow sweep of the hollow, and passed over the fallen pine without a pause.

The goblin's head swung past him and kept walking, and Alaric rose out of cover and threw the lance. Fire tore across the thirty paces between them with a hiss like a poker plunged in water and took the creature square in the back. It lifted off its feet — small, light, burned — and struck a pine trunk and slid down it, and the green lantern rolled free into the needles and guttered there, still glowing, lighting the underside of the branches. The goblin did not move again. The smell of scorched flesh drifted through the cold under the pines. Then nothing. The forest took the sound back. The jay called once more, far off, and was answered this time by only another jay. Alaric stood with the staff raised a moment longer, listening. No second set of feet, no answering cry from the direction of the warrens. Whatever the thing had been — a scout, a lantern-carrier following its own tracks home — it had walked alone. Something settled into him as the tension drained: a warmth behind the eyes, a steadiness, the sense of the world's patterns sitting a little easier in his mind than they had at dawn. The lance had come faster, cleaner. He knew without being told he had stepped up a level. On the body, when he looked, there was little enough: a crude knife, its blade snapped near the hilt, and a few coppers in a greasy knot of rag. He left the body where it lay and kept clear of the lantern's green light pooling in the needles.

RECOVERY — HP 80→85/85, MP 56→87/104
He picked a spot against the fallen pine where the dead goblin and its lantern sat out of his eyeline, laid the staff across his knees, and let the stillness have him. The hollow did what hollows do. A wren worked the bramble bank, fussing and scolding. The stream talked to itself at the edge of hearing. Once a cloud crossed the sun and the whole wood went a shade colder and grayer, then brightened again as if nothing had happened. He ate, drank a mouthful from his waterskin, and watched the needles at his feet the way a man watches nothing in particular. The green lantern burned on the whole time, gutterless and patient, until at some point in the second hour it simply went out — no flicker, no warning — and left the day's ordinary light looking thin and gold by contrast. Warmth came back into him slowly, the way a fire takes on a wet log. First the tightness behind his eyes loosened, and the deep tiredness of the casting drained down his arms and out through his fingers into the ground. Then something better: the well filling. Cold and clean and bottomless, rising by slow degrees until the patterns sat ready at the surface again, a dozen lances' worth of it waiting on his call. By the time the light had tilted well past noon he felt whole — better than whole, steady, the ache of the morning gone from his shoulders. The dead goblin hadn't moved. Nothing else had come to move it. The tracks still ran north into the pines, toward Mossback Warrens, exactly where they had led. It was a little past mid-afternoon, and the light would start failing in three or four hours.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
He picked a spot against the fallen pine where the dead goblin and its lantern sat out of his eyeline, laid the staff across his knees, and let the stillness have him.

The hollow did what hollows do. A wren worked the bramble bank, fussing and scolding. The stream talked to itself at the edge of hearing. Once a cloud crossed the sun and the whole wood went a shade colder and grayer, then brightened again as if nothing had happened. He ate, drank a mouthful from his waterskin, and watched the needles at his feet the way a man watches nothing in particular.

The green lantern burned on the whole time, gutterless and patient, until at some point in the second hour it simply went out — no flicker, no warning — and left the day's ordinary light looking thin and gold by contrast.

Warmth came back into him slowly, the way a fire takes on a wet log. First the tightness behind his eyes loosened, and the deep tiredness of the casting drained down his arms and out through his fingers into the ground. Then something better: the well filling. Cold and clean and bottomless, rising by slow degrees until the patterns sat ready at the surface again, a dozen lances' worth of it waiting on his call. By the time the light had tilted well past noon he felt whole — better than whole, steady, the ache of the morning gone from his shoulders.

The dead goblin hadn't moved. Nothing else had come to move it. The tracks still ran north into the pines, toward Mossback Warrens, exactly where they had led.

It was a little past mid-afternoon, and the light would start failing in three or four hours.

The footprints ran straight through, north into the pines — but once he looked past them, other marks came out of the weave. Older tracks, days old, pressed hard: goblin feet, several sets, all of a size, packed into a beaten line like a cattle path. Not one scout's route. Three he could see. The lean-tos could hold more. The beaten foot-road came out of the fold and ran on north past the camp, deeper into the trees, toward where the ground rose into a long moss-grown hill — the Warrens itself, if the Guild's description held, half a day's walk from Ashbridge and off the old quarry track, which meant this was its edge. He went down the slope to the camp, one hand pressed to his side, and worked through it the way a man does when he wants to be thorough — the lean-tos first, then the fire pit's edge, then the clutter around the peat stack, then the bodies. It was mostly nothing. Hides gone stiff and stinking, half-scraped. A cook pot blackened through. Knots of dry grass used for bedding, cracked clay bowls, a smell of old smoke and worse soaked into everything. The goblins' belts and pouches held nothing but the few coppers already counted, gristle, and a bird's knuckle bone bored through and worn smooth — a trinket, or a charm, worthless either way. He turned over the peat stack's slabs and checked under the lean-to posts. Whatever a camp like this had owned, either the three of them had carried it or there had never been anything worth carrying. Nothing new. What lay there was what lay there: three dead goblins, somebody's ruined supper, and a fire going grey. While he stood among it, the light over the western hills had changed. Clouds were stacking up beyond Duskreach's ridgeline, low and bruise-dark, and the wind that had been carrying the smoke off the camp was cooler than it had been an hour ago. The first far-off mutter of it hadn't reached him yet, but the sky said it would. The camp offered no roof worth the name. His own blood was drying stiff at his waist, and the road home ran back the way he'd come, out of the fold and across the open ground toward town — a walk that looked, just now, like a race with the weather.

He turned over the peat stack's slabs and checked under the lean-to posts. Whatever a camp like this had owned, either the three of them had carried it or there had never been anything worth carrying. Nothing new. What lay there was what lay there: three dead goblins, somebody's ruined supper, and a fire going grey. While he stood among it, the light over the western hills had changed. Clouds were stacking up beyond Duskreach's ridgeline, low and bruise-dark, and the wind that had been carrying the smoke off the camp was cooler than it had been an hour ago. The first far-off mutter of it hadn't reached him yet, but the sky said it would. The camp offered no roof worth the name. His own blood was drying stiff at his waist, and the road home ran back the way he'd come, out of the fold and across the open ground toward town — a walk that looked, just now, like a race with the weather.

The rain found its rhythm within the first half mile — a steady, drumming downpour that turned the track to a slick ribbon of mud and made the dark come down early. Alaric walked with the staff in one hand and his collar up, and the storm took the rest of his attention. Thunder rolled along the ridgeline behind him. Water ran off his chin and soaked through the traveler's clothes in the first hour; after that it hardly mattered. There was nothing drier to get to. The way east was empty. No carts, no lanterns, no one fool enough to be out in it, and the ground on either side of the track dissolved into grey dark where the scrub started. Once something small broke cover ahead of him and splashed away through the wet grass — a hare, or the shape of one — and once a bolt of lightning walked the horizon far to the south and showed him a country of low hills and rain for the length of a heartbeat. Otherwise the walk was mud, wind, and his own breath. He ate nothing and passed nothing worth stopping for. The storm did its worst and settled, past midnight, into a colder, finer rain that hissed instead of roared. It was in that quieter wet, deep in the night, that he came off the old quarry track and found the hill the Guild's directions had promised: a round-shouldered rise standing alone off the east side of the way, dark with old growth, and green — even in the dark, even in the rain — with a moss that grew on it thicker than moss had any right to grow, sheathing the stones and the tree roots and the slope itself in wet velvet. Down at its foot, half-sheltered under an outthrust lip of rock, a dark break in the hillside breathed cold air out at him. The mouth of the Warrens. A short flight of worn steps led down into it, and from somewhere below, under the rain's hiss, came the faintest sound of water moving through stone.

It was in that quieter wet, deep in the night, that he came off the old quarry track and found the hill the Guild's directions had promised: a round-shouldered rise standing alone off the east side of the way, dark with old growth, and green — even in the dark, even in the rain — with a moss that grew on it thicker than moss had any right to grow, sheathing the stones and the tree roots and the slope itself in wet velvet.

Down at its foot, half-sheltered under an outthrust lip of rock, a dark break in the hillside breathed cold air out at him. The mouth of the Warrens. A short flight of worn steps led down into it, and from somewhere below, under the rain's hiss, came the faintest sound of water moving through stone.

ENTERED — Mossback Warrens, Level 1 · Rank F
The steps went down under the rock lip and the rain shut off behind him like a door closing. Cold air rose to meet it, smelling of wet earth and something greener underneath, and his footsteps rang hollow on stone worn slick by boots and weather both. The palisade came at the bottom of the stairs — a crude wall of sharpened logs closing the passage, with a gate of lashed poles in its middle, standing open. Beside it, sheltered under a lean-to of bark, an old man sat on a stool with a ledger open on his knees and a shuttered lantern at his feet, and he looked up as the light found Alaric's wet outline. "Guild?" Alaric showed the mark on him and the old man grunted, licked a stub of pencil, and made his entry without ceremony. "Warrens entry, one. Name?" He took the answer down in a scrawl. "Eight inside at once, that's the rule. Back out through this gate when you're done or half-done, either way, and say so. If you're carried out, they'll say it for you." He closed the ledger on his knee and went back to his lantern as if Alaric had already left. "Level one's down the main run. Keep to the big tunnel and you can't miss it." Past the gate the hill swallowed everything. The main passage ran down and down, its walls sheathed in that same wet green moss, glowing faintly where it grew thickest — enough light to walk by, barely, and the sound of water grew with every step until it was everywhere, running somewhere below through channels in the stone. Goblin work showed soon enough: shored tunnels, pegs, a rope strung along one wall, a stack of firewood gone moldy in an alcove. Fifty paces on, the passage opened into a room, and here the company before him had left their mark. Two goblins lay where they'd been dropped, days dead by the smell, one scorched black across the chest and one simply crumpled. Old scorch stains crawled up the walls. Nothing had touched the bodies since. Beyond the room the main tunnel forked, a three-way split around a mound of packed earth, and from the left-hand branch, faint under the water-noise, came a rhythmic knock — wood on wood, patient, like someone driving stakes.

The wave went out from him where he stood — a ring of raw arcane force that crossed the chamber without caring about mud or stream, and it took them both. It caught the shrieking spearman mid-step and slammed the breath sideways out of it, knocking it back a stagger against the fish-trap stakes; it caught the second one rounding the channel's edge and folded it half over with a grunt of hurt surprise. Both held their feet. Both held their spears. And both came on. The bigger one reached him first, mud spraying, and drove its spear in under his guard — a hard punch of rusted point into his side, tearing through cloth and skin, a hot line of pain that stole his breath. Then the smaller one was there too, shrieking still, and its thrust raked across him lower down, opening a second cut along his hip. Blood ran warm down into his waistband. The two goblins stood on him now, close enough to smell — wet fur, mud, old fish — spears drawn back for the next stroke, yellow eyes bright with the courage of numbers. The smaller one's arm hung oddly at its side where the wave had taken it. The bigger one breathed through its teeth, one hand pressed a moment to its own ribs before the spear came back up.

extra.display_text:
The darker run took him down at a shallow grade, the moss-light thinning until his steps sounded louder than the dripping. The tunnel bent twice, past a clause of old claw tracks in the mud and a broken fish spear someone had left where it fell — passed without a stop — and then opened. The chamber ahead was rounder, drier, higher-ceilinged than the last. Goblin work covered it, but older: a cold firepit ringed with flat stones, a heap of woven bedding gone to mold, racks and stakes and a leaning palisade of sharpened poles against one wall as if something bigger had once been kept behind them. Nobody was behind it now. The space stood empty, the air stale with old smoke and old fur, and across the far wall the goblins had painted their tally in white mud — strokes and circles, meaning what it meant to them. The firepit held the only thing of note: half-buried in the ash, a small clay pot, stoppered with wax. Around it, pressed into the floor's dry mud, prints crossed and crossed again — goblin-small, and one set broader than any goblin foot he had seen so far. Beyond the tally wall, two ways went on: a narrower passage angling left, breathing faintly cooler air, and a wider one right, its floor worn smoother by traffic.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The darker run took him down at a shallow grade, the moss-light thinning until his steps sounded louder than the dripping. The tunnel bent twice, past a clause of old claw tracks in the mud and a broken fish spear someone had left where it fell — passed without a stop — and then opened.

The chamber ahead was rounder, drier, higher-ceilinged than the last. Goblin work covered it, but older: a cold firepit ringed with flat stones, a heap of woven bedding gone to mold, racks and stakes and a leaning palisade of sharpened poles against one wall as if something bigger had once been kept behind them. Nobody was behind it now. The space stood empty, the air stale with old smoke and old fur, and across the far wall the goblins had painted their tally in white mud — strokes and circles, meaning what it meant to them.

The firepit held the only thing of note: half-buried in the ash, a small clay pot, stoppered with wax. Around it, pressed into the floor's dry mud, prints crossed and crossed again — goblin-small, and one set broader than any goblin foot he had seen so far.

Beyond the tally wall, two ways went on: a narrower passage angling left, breathing faintly cooler air, and a wider one right, its floor worn smoother by traffic.
